data_caveats: The 18 ascent records are individual mountain ascents expanded from the source chronology: 14 distinct peaks plus four repeat ascents of Nanga Parbat, Everest, Gasherbrum I and Gasherbrum II. The cumulative chart counts only the first ascent of each distinct peak.

The Annapurna summit position is disputed. The American Alpine Journal contemporary account and Himalayan Database record the 24 April 1985 ascent as successful; the later 8000ers.com analysis offers a competing interpretation based on photographs and topographic analysis, while acknowledging uncertainty around cornices, imagery and summit definition.
The 16 ft / 4.9 m vertical shortfall is attributed to the research interpretation as reported by Outside; it is not an independently established measurement of Messner's exact position.
The 305 m figure refers to the approximate segment from C0 to the Ridge Junction described in the 8000ers.com study, not the entire summit ridge.
The Annapurna ridge profile is an editorial schematic, not a measured elevation profile, surveyed cross-section, GPS track or exact route reconstruction.

In 2023, Guinness changed its recognition of the first climber to reach the true summits of all 14, naming Ed Viesturs retroactively; its earlier legacy record still recognises Messner's 1986 achievement. Messner and Kammerlander disputed the analysis, the UIAA defended Messner, and ANSA later reported a revision in Jurgalski's position. Do not collapse the record-keeping decision into a definitive historical verdict.

The 8000ers.com topography report discusses cornices, changing snow conditions, incomplete imagery and the possibility of a summit tolerance zone. The report cautions against simply dismissing all historical summit claims.

The Nanga Parbat account identifies Günther Messner's death during the descent as a defining tragedy. The exact circumstances became the subject of a long-running dispute among expedition members. The discovery and later burial of his remains on the Diamir Face in 2005 supported an important part of Reinhold's account but did not resolve every question.
Frostbite and amputation details are attributed to Reinhold Messner's own retrospective account, not presented as an independently audited medical record.
The central Messner Mountain Museum at Sigmundskron opened in 2006 after five years of construction; the wider museum project developed over a longer period.
Wikipedia says Messner wrote more than 80 books; his official biography says over 50. Avoid presenting one total as definitive without defining the bibliography.

Antarctica 2,800 km is supported by the American Alpine Journal; Greenland 2,200 km is listed in Messner's official chronology; Gobi about 2,000 km is listed by the user-supplied Wikipedia snapshot. These distances are not necessarily measured on comparable bases.
Peak heights follow the user-supplied Wikipedia snapshot's table; other sources may use differing measurements and conventions.
Summit coordinates are approximate map-placement points, not surveyed positions, GPS tracks or expedition routes. Geographic boundaries are supplied by world-atlas using Natural Earth data.

Noshaq: the 1973 American Alpine Journal report confirms Messner's summit with three companions on 11 August 1972 and describes his technical direction of the expedition. It does not support describing this as the first ascent of Noshaq.

Aconcagua: the 1975 American Alpine Journal report says the central South Face route had first been climbed by the French in 1954; the 1974 Tirolean team sought to straighten its upper section, and Messner continued alone to the summit. Do not call this the first ascent of the South Face.

Chamlang: Douglas Scott's 1982 American Alpine Journal report describes the 1981 north-face climb to P7010, one of the central summits, while identifying the main summit as P7319. The project card refers specifically to the P7010 point, not a summit of the main peak.

Seven Summits: there are competing list definitions. The Bass list includes Kosciuszko; the Carstensz/Messner list substitutes Carstensz Pyramid (Puncak Jaya). Avoid implying that the phrase has only one definition or that Messner was the first person to complete the challenge.

The 7summits.com page is a specialist list database and is used as a cross-check for list completion, while the 1991 Alpine Journal article by Oswald Oelz provides contemporary context for the two list variants.

The Mountain Wilderness organisation describes Messner as instrumental in its creation and involved in its early actions; its own history identifies him among the first international guarantors. The project uses this narrower description rather than simply calling him a founder.
The 2010 Piolet d'Or career award is confirmed by the award organisation's own recipient page.
The European Parliament profile confirms Messner's Greens/EFA membership from 20 July 1999 to 19 July 2004; this is the precise institutional service period used in the project.
The Seven Summits card distinguishes the Bass and Carstensz/Messner variants. It does not claim Messner invented the challenge or was the first person to complete every version.
